key_claims.claim: Mage: The Ascension was first published on August 19, 1993 at Gen Con, making it the third game in the World of Darkness series after Vampire: The Masquerade and Werewolf: The Apocalypse.

The core metaphysical premise of Mage is that reality is shaped by collective human belief (the Consensus), and mages are people who have 'Awakened' to this truth and can reshape reality through will—but face Paradox when they contradict what billions of Sleepers believe is possible.

The Sons of Ether defected from the Technocracy in 1904 after the Union voted to remove the luminiferous ether from the Consensus (following the Michelson-Morley experiments). As a 'parting shot,' they slipped relativity and quantum mechanics into the Consensus.

The Virtual Adepts defected from the Technocracy in 1961, reportedly spurred by the Technocracy's treatment of Alan Turing. They joined the Council of Nine Traditions through the Sons of Ether's sponsorship.
Changeling: The Dreaming was published in July 1995 as the fifth World of Darkness game, and borrowed heavily from Neil Gaiman's The Sandman and Neverwhere.

In Changeling lore, the 1969 moon landing generated such a surge of human wonder and Glamour that it reopened the gates to Arcadia, allowing the sidhe nobility to return to Earth after centuries of absence—an event called the Resurgence.

The returning sidhe's attempt to reclaim rulership over commoner changelings sparked the Accordance War in the early 1970s, which ended with High King David Ardry ap Gwydion establishing the Parliament of Dreams as a compromise.

Mage: The Ascension was cited by developer Phil Brucato as 'a major inspiration behind the Matrix movies,' with the game's themes of awakening to hidden reality and fighting a system of control predating the 1999 film by six years.
key_claims.confidence: Medium-High (based on developer statement, not Wachowski confirmation)

key_claims.claim: The Shattering (1200-1400 AD) was the catastrophic severing of the Dreaming from mundane reality, associated with the Black Plague. Most sidhe fled to Arcadia; commoners who remained developed the Changeling Way ritual to survive by bonding fae souls with human bodies.

Banality in Changeling represents not just disbelief but the mundane forces of modern life—'television, doctors, lines at the bank, money machines, traffic, malls'—and if a changeling's Banality exceeds their Glamour, they slip into the Mists and forget their fae nature.
